utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. You may be seated. Good morning ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning court reporters and legal assistants; good morning. I see that the Office of the Prosecution is present, as well as the Defence counsel. Good morning to the accused. And as I have already informed you, Judge Fouad Riad continues to be absent and we are going to continue working within the same framework that we adopted last week. I think that the parties accepted and were in agreement. Is that the case, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Defence? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So we're going to resume the hearings by having the witness brought in, who we will continue to listen to her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Susic. Can you hear me? Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a nice weekend here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you feel rested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're going to continue with your testimony. Who will be asking questions? I think it is Mr. Saxon. You have the floor, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Susic.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, just before we adjourned on Friday afternoon, you had described your arrival at the Omarska camp on the afternoon of the 24th of June, 1992. Besides the female detainees in the restaurant that you saw, who else, if anyone, did you speak to on that first day in the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many women and there were several guards, and after an hour or two, after my arrival at the restaurant, Zeljko Meakic came. He was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Meakic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were colleagues at work. He worked in the Omarska police station as the commander of the Omarska department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did Mr. Meakic say to you on that first day in the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came up to me and he said, "Sifeta, come with me." He put his hand on my shoulder and in his other hand he held his jacket, thrown over his shoulder. He took me to an office upstairs. I was crying. I sat there for a few minutes and he said, "I was extremely surprised to learn that you did not sign loyalty to the Serb authorities." I answered, "I wouldn't have done that if the Muslims had asked it of me," and I continued crying. I don't remember the rest of our conversation. I was there for another 10 or 15 minutes, after which Meakic took me back to the restaurant to join with the other women.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, what was Zeljko Meakic's position at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did you think that Mr. Meakic was the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I noticed that he had an office where -- I don't know how to put it -- he was in charge. If it had been somebody else's office, he probably wouldn't have taken me there. Furthermore, in the 20 or so years I had worked in the SUP, we had military exercises on several occasions, and we all had decisions on our wartime assignments. And I remember well that on such occasions we were engaged in the same sort of activities as in peacetime. Starting from me personally, I continued doing my job; my boss, the SUP secretary, the commander of the police station of Prijedor. So all our war assignments coincided with those we had in peacetime, so I assumed that he continued performing the same duties when war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you assumed that Mr. Meakic had a parallel position when the armed conflict began in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he was there. The Omarska police station no longer existed; instead, everything happened in the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Meakic had an office at the Omarska camp. Where did Mr. Meakic have this office?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upstairs, to the right. In front of the office there were -- prior to the office there were two toilets. Then there were two offices. But I can't say for sure whether I went into the first or the second, but I know that that is where later I would see Meakic and Mladjo Radic and Kvocka, Miroslav and Prcac, Drago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Susic. We're going to get to that. When you say Mr. Meakic used an office that was upstairs, do you mean upstairs in the building where the restaurant was?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So would that office have been on the first floor of that building?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you recall, Ms. Susic, what was across the corridor from the office or offices that Zeljko Meakic used?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two other offices in which women slept. I was in one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Susic, who else, if anyone, also held positions of authority at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the deputy of Zeljko Meakic, and he was Miroslav Kvocka, and his assistant or maybe he had some other title, it was Mlado Radic, because I know in the Prijedor police station. We had the commander, the assistant and the deputy. Whether those same positions existed in the Omarska camp is something I cannot say for sure, but I know that there was the position of commander and deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And approximately how long did Miroslav Kvocka remain as deputy commander of the Omarska camp while you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly. I can't say exactly but maybe for two weeks or three, but not for long. And when I stopped seeing him, Drago Prcac appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we get to that point, I have some more questions for you. How often would you see Miroslav Kvocka during those two or three weeks early on when you were detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly how many times, but I know that I did see him. In the evening when we would go to the room that we slept in, he would usually be in one of those offices, and on several occasions, I spoke to him when I could, on the way from the room to the toilet. If the door of that -- of one of those offices was open, I would always go in and ask them to give us some hygienic materials, specifically I addressed Kvocka several days after my arrival asking whether he had any -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him whether he had antibiotics because I had a high fever and a very sore throat. He told me he didn't. Maybe a day later I asked Mlado Radic the same question and he said he didn't have any, but two or three days after talking to Miroslav Kvocka, he came when I was upstairs in the room. Whether we met in the corridor or I went inside to his office, I can't remember exactly, but he said, "Sifeta, I've got some antibiotics. I have received some and I brought them for you," and he gave them to me. And he said that an acquaintance of mine, Fiketa Oklopcic who is his neighbour living next door to him had sent it for me. He went on to tell me that the day before, she had come to talk to him because she had heard that she was -- that I was in Omarska, and he said, "Yes, she is. She has asked me for antibiotics. I didn't have any." And then she said, "I have some, please take them for her," and he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Susic. Ms. Susic, you said that you spoke to Mr. Kvocka in the office that he used. Where was that office located?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the way from mine. There were two offices that they used, but I cannot say for sure which one of those two, the first or the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say across the way from mine, do you mean across the way from the room where you and other women slept?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two rooms where the women slept and across the way from those rooms were two offices which were used by the individuals I have mentioned: Meakic, Kvocka, Prcac, Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who, if anyone, replaced Miroslav Kvocka as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say, but I know that after a certain time, I no longer saw him and then Drago Prcac appeared. So I assume, it is my opinion, that Miroslav was replaced or he went of his own free will, but in any event, Drago Prcac took over instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did Drago Prcac use an office in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see him too in one of these two offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, what position, if any, did Mlado Radic hold at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure, but I know that he was there with Meakic, Kvocka, later Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that Mlado Radic was there, where, specifically, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of these two offices that I am referring to all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Susic, did ordinary guards at the Omarska camp use these offices?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large table in front of those offices, and that is where the guards would usually be or sitting around the table or standing around there or downstairs in the restaurant. I don't remember seeing them in these offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The rooms that were across the corridor from these offices, what were they used for?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they were used for. They were just there. What they did there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think my question was perhaps not very clear. Across the corridor from these offices were rooms where the women slept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly. I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand which rooms you were referring to. Yes, the -- I thought you meant the rooms where Meakic, Radic and Kvocka would stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The rooms that the women used as sleeping rooms at night, what were those rooms used for during the day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For questioning because cries, moans could always be heard coming from those rooms which we would clearly hear in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So Ms. Susic, normally what time of day would you usually notice one or more of the camp commanders to be present in the offices that were across the corridor from the women's sleeping rooms?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening about 7.00 when we would be taken from the restaurant to those rooms, we would go to the toilet then, and on the way there, I had many occasions to see them and meet them either going into their offices, coming out or sitting inside with the door open.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, I'd like to ask you to stand up please and remove your headphones, and I'd like to ask you to put on these headphones with the longer cord. Ms. Susic, I'd like you to step over here, please, if you would, and remove the roof of the restaurant building if you could. Ms. Susic, if you could remove the roof and explain where these offices were and where the commander -- where the sleeping rooms were where the women slept. Could you remove the other roof, please? Could the bailiff please remove the other roof?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the restaurant where we would stay and in the evening around 7.00, we would go along this corridor up the steps. This is where the table was where the guards would usually sit. The toilets were here and these were the two offices that were used by Zeljko Meakic, Mlado Radic, Miroslav Kvocka and Drago Prcac, and these were the two offices where the women slept. I slept in this office here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Susic. Would you please sit down now. Ms. Susic, I'm sorry, I'd ask you to please come back to the model. Could you tell the Judges what the numbers are on those rooms that you indicated?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: B10 and -- was the one I slept in, B11 was the other one used by women. Across the corridor were rooms B5 and B4 used by Meakic, Kvocka, Radic, and Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Susic, on your first day in the Omarska camp, the 24th of June, 1992, what physical changes, if any, occurred to you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cried a lot those first few days. I couldn't eat, and I couldn't sleep at all. I would sit up all night with my knees up and my eyes wide open. After two or three days, Biba Harambasic gave me a sleeping pill and believe me, that didn't help, I still couldn't sleep. I got a high fever and I had a very sore throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, did you have any problems with bleeding on the first day of your detention in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe the problems that you had?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first day I arrived at the camp I started to bleed, which didn't stop throughout my stay. The problem was that I hadn't prepared myself for this, because I thought I would be leaving my house for an hour or two. No one explained where they were taking me. I didn't even know that there was a camp in Omarska. I remember that a woman gave me a blouse or a T-shirt of hers that I used instead of a sanitary napkin, and that is why I went into those offices and asked Kvocka, Radic, asking them to give me some cotton wool or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Ms. Susic, when, if ever, did Miroslav Kvocka bring you any sanitary supplies?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get any sanitary supplies, but I got those tablets, those antibiotics that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And had you also asked Mladjo Radic to bring you some antibiotics?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Not to bring them. I thought that perhaps they had some supplies in the office, as well as these sanitary materials which I was looking for. I thought perhaps they had in their offices. But unfortunately I didn't get anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mladjo Radic give you any response when you made that request to him?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just said he didn't have it, he didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where was Mladjo Radic when you made that request to him for antibiotics?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in one of these two offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, were you able to bathe or change your clothes while you were detained at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The water was cold. There were showers. But a change of clothing, I had nothing for a long time. I just had that blouse, skirt, and jacket; nothing else. And much later a relative of mine, Zlata Sarhatlic, sent me a sweatsuit and a packet of sanitary towels and soap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, approximately how many other women were detained with you at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were about 36 in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know the ethnicity of these women?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim. Muslims and Croats, in fewer numbers, and as far as I can recollect, there were two Serb women as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the approximate range of age of these women that were with you at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of different ages. I remember there were some who were underage -- I remember a young girl who was mentally retarded. She told us she went to a special school, and she was underage -- up to the oldest ones, who were in their 60s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The woman who was underage, do you recall her name?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think her name was Azra.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who, if anyone, provided assistance to Azra?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Azra was not in my room; she was in the other room. She had been wounded during the shelling of a village near Prijedor. Whether it was Hambarine or Carakovo, I can't remember. I know that sometimes they would carry her to the toilet. I would meet her in the corridor. I think Suada Ramic would take her to the toilet. She was in the other room too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you think that Suada Ramic would carry Azra to the bathroom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In general, Ms. Susic, where did you and the other female detainees spend your days in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the restaurant and in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at about what time of the afternoon or evening would the women go to their sleeping rooms?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About seven o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during the day, if you know, what was your sleeping room used for?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the questioning of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the evenings, when you went upstairs to your sleeping room, what, if anything, would you find there?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before going to those rooms, the guard would usually come and select two or three women to go upstairs to clean those rooms. I was called out on a number of occasions to do this cleaning. Those premises were bloody. On the tables there were various objects. I remember well. I hadn't been doing the cleaning that day, but when we came in there were some pieces of paper on the table. Whether the interrogators left those papers on purpose or forgot them, I don't know. I remember that one of the women collected those papers and took them to the offices, because we were afraid that they might say that we had read through those documents and we might have certain problems as a result. And I remember very well that on the table in the room I slept in, one day I saw something that looked like a whip. There was a wooden handle wound with string, a very long whip, and at the end of this whip there was a metal ball. One could also find there lead pipes. That day I saw a lead pipe with a diameter something like this and roughly half a metre long. And I also remember very well a yellow cable, which was also very thick. I don't know what it was used for otherwise, but I can only assume what it was used for in the office. And I also recollect well there was an iron metal hanger, clothes hanger, and it was close to a plug. And on this hanger used for umbrellas, there was a wire, and this wire could be plugged into the socket. But at the end there were two separate wires that were wound around this metal part of the hanger used for umbrellas. I assume that they used this. That is what I saw on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Susic.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, at night, while the women were in their sleeping rooms, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard screams throughout the night, groans, cries, shots. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What else happened besides the sounds that you heard at night?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes the women would be called out. Sometimes some of them would come into our room. They would sit around talking to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who would call the women out?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually a guard would come, one of the guards, and I remember on one occasion one of them -- one of the women would be called out frequently during the day and at night, and they would say, "Go to Meakic" or "Zeljko's looking for you," or something like that. And the women would go out and sometimes come back at dawn. I remember on one occasion she came later on. She was all red round the neck and was crying. She didn't say anything and we never asked her anything. We could all only guess what happened to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, when the woman returned to your sleeping room, was it dark or light in the room?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we wouldn't turn the lights off until 11.00. We would sit around talking. And sometimes she would come in during the dark, when we weren't able to see what she looked like when she came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were there times when there was light in the room when this woman returned?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember one particular occasion that -- I remember the light was still on when she came in. She was crying and she was all red round her neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, were there times when you did not look at the women when they were called out or when they returned to the sleeping room?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were times when I didn't look.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did you choose not to look?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always avoided terrible situations and looking at terrible situations, and I just didn't want to look at her because, as I say, I assumed what had happened to the woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, due to the sensitive nature of the next questions that I have, I would ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, we're in public session, you may proceed. Mr. Saxon, if the witness is ready to continue, and may I suggest that you make a little slight breaks to give the witness a chance to recover.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, how did you spend your days in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sitting about in the restaurant and working in the kitchen. I very often volunteered to work in the kitchen. When the guard came to ask which of us women would be working that day, I usually volunteered and said that I wanted to work because I found it easier to work. I would see less, hear less, what was going on, and the time would pass more quickly. But sometimes they wouldn't let me and they would say, "You worked yesterday or the day before. Let somebody else go today."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you use to wash the dishes in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We usually just used cold water. Sometimes we'd heat the water up a little bit on the stove.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have to work all day long washing dishes or could you take a break from time to time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we worked the whole time that the detainees came to what was referred to as lunch. I don't know when this would actually begin, 11.00 and went on until lunch was over. The detainees would come in groups of 30 in a column one by one. They would come in running. They would run into the restaurant. The guards would wait for them there and beat them as soon as they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were there moments when you were able to observe the detainees coming into the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them every day. I would see them much better when I was sitting in the restaurant, then I could see them from the time they entered the restaurant until they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Susic, did you know a man named Husein Crnkic, and I apologise if I'm mispronouncing his name.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Husein Crnkic, yes, he was a mathematics professor at the secondary school. I didn't know him personally, but I knew who he was very well, as a citizen of Prijedor. And as you know, Prijedor was a very small town and mostly we would know each other by sight. And one day when he was going out from lunch he took his shirt, turned his back to us and pushed his shirt down his back. He wanted to -- me to see because on his back between these shoulder-blade bones here, there was a hole. It was almost big enough to fit my whole fist in it and I can't see how he was able to live with a wound that big. What inflicted the wound, I don't know but it was terrible to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, when you observed that wound on the back of Husein Crnkic, approximately how far were you from Mr. Crnkic that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three metres. Because when they came into the restaurant, they would pass by the glass partition where there was a metal barrier. They would go to the kitchen to collect their plates and then they would come back looking from where I was to the left-hand side where the tables were laid for the meal. When they finished their meal, they would return their plates and spoons. So it was in this direction where the tables were. Then they would move down the centre of the restaurant, go around that way and go out of the restaurant so that he was very close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnicity of Husein Crnkic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, prior to the armed conflict, did you know a man named Reuf Travancic? And again I apologise if I'm mispronouncing the person's name.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Reuf Travancic was also a colleague from work. He worked in the crime department. For a time, he was chief of crime technology, and later on he was an inspector for the fire prevention -- in the fire prevention department but he was already retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to ask the usher to place a photograph on the ELMO beside Ms. Susic. Your Honour, this is an original photograph which we would like to return to the witness, and I have made 15 copies to be distributed this morning. I believe one copy will need to be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 3/99 [Realtime transcript read in error "399"], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to correct the mistake in the transcript, it should be Exhibit 3/99.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, could you please take a look at the photograph that's by your side. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When was it taken approximately?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what year it was but I know that it was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who, if anyone, do you recognise in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The man with the glasses is Reuf Travancic. The man -- the person holding him by the hand is myself, that's me. And this is one of our collective celebrations, but where we were celebrating, which restaurant it was, whether it was in town or somewhere else, I really can't remember. I know that we would very often go to a hotel on Mount Kozoro or a hotel in Prijedor to celebrate occasions like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you refer to "One of our a collective celebrations," are you referring to yourself and your colleagues at work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were office parties. The parties of the employees of SUP. We would celebrate the 13th of May for example, the public security day, and the 8th of March, International Women's Day and many other celebrations of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, have you had the original photograph in your possession from approximately the time it was taken?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When, if ever, did you see Reuf Travancic in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in the camp, yes. It could have been the middle or end of July. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where were you that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, I was working in the kitchen like I did on many other days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was cleaning the table next to the wash basin where the detainees returned their plates and spoons after they had finished eating, I saw Drago Prcac. He was moving along the glass partition, the "glass house", and he had under his arm a black book or notebook of some kind. I know that it had black covers. And he was carrying it under his left arm. And he was walking past the "glass house" towards the kitchen and I continued cleaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much time went by, two minutes, five minutes, ten minutes, I finished what I was doing and I went to the toilet. When I went into the toilet, I heard terrible screams and cries and blunt blows. There was a small window high up in the toilet so I could hear all this clearly and it all happened in that section in front of the toilet window. I was very frightened and turned around and went back into the restaurant. Women were already sitting on the table in the restaurant with their heads bowed down in their hands, their heads were bowed down on the table. I sat in the last chair which was empty and looking at it from that position, the kitchen was in front of me and to my left-hand side were the restaurant windows. I put my hands down like this and my -- rested my head on my hands, but with the corner of my eye, I was able to see what was going on next to the restaurant. At one particular moment, I saw a column of people coming one by one, the detainees who were beaten there a moment ago were passing by. The third or fourth in order or perhaps the fifth in line I recognised as Reuf Travancic. He didn't have his glasses. His side of his face turned towards me was covered in blood. He was wearing a white shirt which was all torn, and you could see traces on it, black traces, black marks on that white shirt. The pockets of his trousers --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pockets of his trousers were turned out so that you could see the lining. I turned my head so that I could watch them and see where they were going. They were being taken to the "white house". A woman, I don't know which one, but one of the women would comment and she said, "They've taken them to the white house," and the women who were sitting around opposite me could see the "white house" directly from where they were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Susic, at this time, with the Court's permission and with the usher's assistance, I'd like to place a floor plan on the ELMO by your side. Your Honour this is a copy of what was Prosecution's Exhibit 3/77, however I am going to ask the witness to make some markings on it so it will have to be renumbered 3/100. This was 3/77A, Your Honour, pardon me. Ms. Susic, if you could look over that floor plan and with a pencil or a pen, please mark where you were that morning in the restaurant when you first saw Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't in the morning, it was the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was here somewhere, there was a table there where the detainees, once they had finished eating, would return their empty plates and Drago Prcac was standing here. He was walking past the "glass house" which means that he had to go through the kitchen. The only exit led this way in front of the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, could I stop you there, please. Could you mark with a "P" where you saw Drago Prcac that morning, that afternoon before he left the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was here next to the "glass house", somewhere here approximately in the centre, and I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you put a little one next to that 'S' that you just made, so we'll mark that "S1", thank you. And then where did you go after Mr. Prcac left the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed this way and went to the toilet which was somewhere here. That was where the toilets were opposite the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is that where you were when you first heard the screams and the sounds of beatings?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you mark that place with an "S2". Thank you. And then where on this floor plan did you go next?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed through the kitchen, whether this door or that door, I can't remember, but I know that I walked across the middle of the restaurant very quickly and sat down somewhere here. This is where the women were sitting. And the last chair or the first next to the window was the empty chair where I sat and looked in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you mark with an "S3" the approximate spot where you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you mark with a "T" the area or approximate area where you saw Reuf Travancic pass by that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was here. In this area here. And I saw him through this window here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you place a T there, please. Thank you. When did you see Reuf Travancic next?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for certain that he didn't come to lunch the next day so whether it was two days later or three days later, I can't say for sure. But I saw him wearing that same white shirt, and you could clearly see now the imprints of an army boot, the corrugated rubber of the army boot, and he was all black and blue around the eyes and mouth, and he had bruises all over these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, when, if ever, did you hear screams coming from within the restaurant or administration building itself?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would happen during the interrogations. Sometimes those cries were so loud that they would play music, whether it was the radio or a tape recorder, very loud. But believe me, still those cries of those tortured people could still be heard above the sound of the music.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, did you know any of the persons who carried out the interrogations at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were my colleagues from the crime service, starting from my boss, Ranko Mijic; Vukasin Knezevic; Inspector Nebojsa Tomcic; Nebojsa Babic, inspector; Drago Meakic, a retired inspector; Didakovic [phoen], Obrad, inspector. And every day, except on Saturdays and Sundays, when they came in the morning, they would pass through the restaurant. Every morning this would be, between 8.00 and 9.00. I remember well looking them straight in the eye to see their reactions. Sometimes Drago Meakic or Obrad Despotovic would nod their heads in the direction of the women who were sitting there. Others never even cast a glance in our direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, what was the ethnicity of these former colleagues who worked as interrogators in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you observe any difference in the treatment of detainees after the interrogators left for the day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing, after interrogations, somebody being carried out wrapped in a blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know the person who was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When, if ever, were you interrogated at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. I don't remember exactly what day it was, or rather after how many days after my arrival, but a guard came, called out my name, and told me to go with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me to this office, the one I had spent the night in previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was present in that sleeping room, or office, as it was being used that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Radakovic, who was a teacher of art. I didn't know him personally. And I know before the war he held a managerial post, but I don't remember in which company. And another man whom I didn't know, but whom I would see in front of the restaurant sometimes. He would come out of a car, passenger car, called Stojadin, with Banja Luka licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall the nature of your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, very well. First of all he asked me for my ID card, which I had on me. I gave it to him. This unknown man questioned me; not Dragan Radakovic. And he asked me what I was doing in the camp, why I had been brought there. I said, "You give me an explanation. I am expecting you to give me the answer. I don't know." And I was saying all this through tears. Then he asked me who I have among family members, where they were now and prior to the outbreak of the conflict. I told him everything. I gave him answers to all those questions. At one point he said to me, "You held a rally prior to the actual outbreak of the war." I said, "I never spoke in public anywhere except in the SUP, where we had meetings." And I asked him to tell me where this was that he said I had spoken, but he didn't give me an answer. The next question was: "You don't say hello to your colleagues," and this applied, I remember very well, to the situation when the Serbs took over power. One morning I was in front of the post office and nearby was Radovan Vokic, wearing a uniform, but a new uniform, with the 4 S's on his cap. He was carrying an automatic rifle. I think that's what it was called. And he said to me, "Where are you, friend?" And I answered, "We can't be friends now, when you have taken up arms and are wearing a uniform with that insignia." He laughed and I passed by. And that was what he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, during your interrogation, were you threatened in any way?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not threatened. I remember that Dragan Radakovic, in answer to my question as to how long I would be kept there and why I had been brought to Omarska, he said, "This is a military camp," or something to that effect. And I said, "I'm not a soldier. I'm not in uniform. I was brought here from my house, from my own bed." His answer was, "Then you will probably be released and you will go back home." However, it took some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, from the windows of the restaurant building at the Omarska camp, were you able to see the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You were able to see prisoners going into the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything outside around the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Piles of bodies, behind the "white house," in front of the "white house," every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was Mladjo Kvocka ever present nearby those piles of bodies?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see bodies disposed of? The bodies that were laying around the "white house" at the Omarska camp, did you ever see those bodies being disposed of in any way?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember one night, or rather a morning, it had just dawned; dawn had broken. My place in the room was just below the window. And Tesma Elezovic was next to me, and she looked through the window every morning and she would comment on the number of bodies and who was being taken away. That morning she grabbed me by the arm and said, "You have to see this." And indeed it was horrific. It wasn't a pile; it was a hill of bodies. There were three trucks of yellow/orange colour. I shall never forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And sometimes they wouldn't have time to take away all those bodies, and then they would continue doing it while we went down to the restaurant, so we could see it even from closer up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, approximately how far was the "white house" from the restaurant building, if you can give an estimate?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. I don't know. But I know I could see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, were there persons that you knew who disappeared from the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many of my colleagues from work and also citizens I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know a man Ago Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well. He was a colleague of mine. He was head of the department for economic crime. We were taken away on the same day. When I was taken into custody in SUP, he was already there. He was standing next to the counter of the operations room, leaning on the wall. I remember well. He had a brown leather short jacket and a striped -- horizontally striped T-shirt. I remember that day. It was the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before you go on -- Ms. Susic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Did you also know a man named Mirsad Alisic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, extremely well. He too was an inspector in the crime service. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when did you last see Ago Sadikovic and Mirsad Alisic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the end of July. I think it was a Monday, about 4.30 or 5.00. I don't know exactly. First I saw a soldier come to the "glass house" and take Ago Sadikovic out. I looked him straight in the eye, but he never looked at the women. He was carrying his jacket in his hand and a plastic bag. And he was taken away down the corridor, where the toilets were. And it occurred to me as we had come together that I might be taken away as well. When I looked up again, Ago was somewhere in front of the "white house." He was being taken towards the "red house." And I didn't look any longer, and I never saw him again. His wife would come to my apartment when I was released, and she would ask me whether I knew anything. I couldn't say anything. I just said, "He was there and then one day I stopped seeing him."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, if you recall --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That same day --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there another prisoner led away with Ago Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That afternoon they took away other detainees as well. As I was crying there, somebody said, "They're taking Mirsad Alisic. I turned around and saw him next to the pista. He was being taken towards the restaurant building. A soldier was going behind him. And I shall never forget that day. That day Mirso was the last in the group for lunch. I was sitting in the restaurant. And he was the last collecting crumbs from his plate and he ran off to catch up with the group. And our eyes met and we smiled at each other, and that was the last time I saw him. He wore a pale green T-shirt and an unbuttoned white shirt with pink stripes. He was dressed in the same way when he was being taken to the restaurant building. I don't know where they took him, but five or ten minutes later, I can't say exactly, I saw him again escorted by a soldier, crossing the pista, I think, going towards the hangar, as they called the building. I don't know exactly. I turned around. I risked anything happening to me because I wanted to see what would happen. He reached the first entrance. The soldier stayed outside waiting. He went in and came out carrying a plastic bag. And he was taken to the "red house" and I never saw him again. That day, Dr. Osman Mahmuljin was also taken there, who was brought to the camp on the same day as I was and Ago Sadikovic and some others. I remember Dr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Susic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, I'm sorry for interrupting you. Do you need -- how much more time do you need to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be a convenient moment to have a break to give the witness a rest, and also the Defence can organise themselves for the cross-examination. So we're now going to have a half-hour break and we will resume after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susic, I'm sorry, Ms. Susic. [As interpreted]. Is there anything wrong with the accused, why they are not here? I see in the transcript it says "Ms. Susic", I was addressing myself to the registrar, not to the witness, to inquire about the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. I am now addressing the witness. Ms. Susic, you will continue to answer questions put to you by Mr. Saxon and I note with pleasure that we have in the courtroom Mr. Niemann for the record. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, before we took a break, you described how you saw Ago Sadikovic and Mirso Alisic being taken towards the "red house" one day in July. Who else, if anyone, did you see taken towards the "red house" on that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, Dr. Osman Mahmuljin who was brought to the camp on the same day as I. Dr. Pasic, who used to work in Kozarac, he was a doctor, a physician, and there were other -- others. I can't recollect their names, but I know that they were taken across the pista in the direction of the "red house".

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd ask that Exhibit 3/82 please be shown to the witness and placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Susic, if you would, please, look at that photograph and perhaps point for the Judges where you saw these men and where they were being led towards?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well seeing Ago Sadikovic here in this area. Mirso Alisic, I saw him first. He was here in the middle. When he was coming out of this building where the restaurant was, I saw him again here in the middle between the restaurant and this hangar, I think they called it the hangar, and the soldiers stopped right here in front of the door waited for Mirso. When Mirso came out with a white plastic bag, and he was taken in this direction. But from the place where I was sitting, I could see in front of the "red house" a corner of the concrete slab. I assume it was the door, and there was a hedge here and I saw a corner of this area so it was in this area that I saw them being led away. But I didn't see whether they entered the "red house" or not because I couldn't see that. It was hidden from my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, could you simply point out which building was the "red house," what was what you refer to as the "red house"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this house here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the men that you saw being escorted towards the "red house" on that day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you observe about their appearance?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all beaten up. They had long hair, beards. On one occasion, making a statement, I said that all those men hardly appeared to be human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, have any of those men been seen again?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Did you ask me specifically for these individuals that I have now named or about the detainees in general how they looked?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the specific individuals that you saw led to the red house on that day in July.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that neither Ago Sadikovic nor Mirso Alisic had a beard. They had normal length hair and they were clean shaven, but I thought you were asking me about the detainees in general, and that is why I described them as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, my question was: To your knowledge, have any of these men, Ago Sadikovic, Mirso Alisic or the two doctors that you have mentioned, have any of them been seen again since the day you saw them taken to the "red house"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw them again in the camp and after that I left the camp, I said that Ago Sadikovic's wife came to see me and inquire about him which means that she didn't know where he was either. Dr. Mahmuljin never appeared again while I was in Prijedor. He was the brother of my cousin, and I know that they inquired about him but I couldn't tell them either. Unfortunately when I left Bosnia, this cousin of mine Faruk Rizic and his wife Rizic, whose maiden name was Mahmuljin, and her sister, who is Fadila Mahmuljin, who worked in the Prijedor hospital as a nurse, they were killed in their apartment in the house in which they lived. They were not killed, they were mutilated. I was told this by a person who buried them and I know that Osman never appeared again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the usher could please remove that photograph from the ELMO. And if these three original photographs could be placed on the ELMO. And Your Honour, I will distribute around the courtroom photocopies of the original photographs so that one of the photocopies could be marked I believe as Prosecution Exhibit 3/101, and so that subsequently the original photographs could be returned to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, if you look at the photograph in the upper right-hand corner, yes, that photograph there; do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where was it taken?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long time prior to the outbreak of the war, and it was also a celebration, a party of the workers employed in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who, if anyone, do you recognise in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Ago Sadikovic who disappeared in the Omarska camp. Next to him is Ilija Bijelic who was an inspector who would come to the Omarska camp to interrogate people. This is Nebojsa Tomcic who would also come to Omarska to interrogate. And this is Nebojsa Babic, though you can't see him well. He was also an inspector that would come to Omarska and Zivko Jovic whom I saw once, I'm sure -- I'm not sure whether it was twice. I saw him in the kitchen. I was cleaning the floor and he passed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could direct your attention to the photograph beneath that, beneath the photograph you just described, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was also probably a celebration of the 8th of March in one of the offices of the crime service. This is Alisic, Mirso, who disappeared in Omarska and this is me. This is inspector Ilija Bijelic who also came to Omarska as an interrogator.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you turn to the photograph that is on the far left.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Meho Mahmutovic, a policeman who worked in the traffic police. I know he was in the camp, but one day I simply stopped seeing him. When I left the camp, when I was collecting documents to be able to leave Prijedor, I met his sister, Nada, in front of the Red Cross, and she inquired about him, whether I had seen him, whether I knew anything about him. My answer was, "I saw him, and one day I stopped seeing him."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, where did you see Meho Mahmutovic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the restaurant, when he came for so-called lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So one day did Meho Mahmutovic simply stop coming for meals?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stopped seeing him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Susic, have these three photographs, the originals, been in your possession since the approximate times when they were taken?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the photographs could be removed, please. Perhaps if the usher could place Exhibit 3/99, which is the floor plan, back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, if I could please redirect your attention to the afternoon when you saw Drago Prcac pass through the restaurant area when you were present. And you have already marked this Exhibit, and you had marked a "P" where you had seen Dragoljub Prcac walking by in the restaurant. And you indicated at one point that Drago Prcac exited the restaurant. Can you point out on that exhibit where Drago Prcac was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part here, when he was passing by the "glass house" in the direction of the kitchen. But I didn't see him go out, because there was a door here for exiting, but I didn't see him come back either. So my assumption is that he passed through the kitchen and he went out here, where the men were beaten. Because I remember when I was brought to the camp, I and the other detainees were met by Miroslav Kvocka. So in my opinion, it was quite logical that these detainees must have been met by someone when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention, Ms. Susic, to the corridor that is marked as A24. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you at any time see Dragoljub Prcac pass into or through that corridor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I saw him here, next to the "glass house," and he went in the direction of the kitchen. And I was here. I was cleaning this table here, and I didn't see him come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Susic, when were you released from the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 3rd of August, 1992, early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened that morning?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we came down from the rooms we slept in to the restaurant, Zeljko Meakic came with a list and said, "The women whose names I call out should go out and board the bus." We didn't know who would be called out, nor where we would be taken, so we could neither be happy nor upset. When my name was called out, I went out, and close to the pista was a bus. Next to the bus was Drago Prcac, and going up to the bus I asked him, "Drago, where are you taking us?" And he said, "Siva, I don't know." I got into the bus, and with the other women we were wondering where we would be taken. Whether it was salvation or the worst, we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, where did you go after Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was your physical and psychological condition when you arrived at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was terrible. We didn't know what lay in store for us. But when I got there and when I saw people moving around a little, it was much better than it was in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your own physical and psychological health when you arrived at the Trnopolje camp. How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was frightened, exhausted. In brief, I didn't know what our arrival in Trnopolje meant, whether we would be sent somewhere else or returned home. It was a feeling of uncertainty, because terrible things happened there too. We were told about them by the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how long were you detained in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of August I was released from the camp, together with many other women. There was a room there where Red Cross employees were present and an acquaintance of mine. I remember her first name was Blanka. I've forgotten her last name. She had some forms into which she entered the name, date of birth, and she wrote down that I had been there in some kind of a collection centre from the 3rd to 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where did you go after you left the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went home. However, on the door of my apartment another name plate was attached, so I couldn't go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the name on that name plate?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb name, but I don't remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how long after that day did you remain in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed with my brother, but then I did return to my apartment, because the man who had written his name on the door hadn't moved in. Before that, my brother and a neighbour, a Serb, Sretko Muzgonja, had taken all my things and moved them to my parents' home. I took all my things back and went into the apartment, but I was afraid, and I spent many nights at my brother's. I don't remember the exact date, whether it was the 15th or the 14th of November, 1992, when, organised by the Prijedor Red Cross, I left Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why did you decide to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I had no job. Secondly, there was fear. Strange things were still happening. Very often I had been disturbed by phone, even before the war and after I came out of the camp. I remember well one evening somebody phoned my brother. It was a quarter to 10.00. The curfew in force. My brother was living several buildings away from mine. He ran up in haste and said that somebody had called up, introduced himself as an Izet, a friend of mine, and I knew no Izet, and he said, "Sifeta will be taken to Mount Vlasic tonight for an exchange." And my brother went back home. I stayed in my own apartment. Then this neighbour, Sretko Muzgonja, said, "Don't be afraid. Nothing will happen to you. I'll take care of you." And indeed nobody did come. So this was merely a provocation. Somebody wanted to frighten me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, why would the mention of Mount Vlasic, and an exchange at Mount Vlasic, frighten someone like yourself?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard once that a bus -- not one, several buses, when they were transporting people towards Travnik, they probably had to go via Vlasic. There were 200 or 300 people, and apparently they were executed there. And I also know from the Omarska camp, when people were taken for an exchange, all traces of them were lost. There was Edna Markovic and Sadeta Medjunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, before you left Prijedor, what steps did you have to take before you were able to leave?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to collect a number of certificates. First of all, I had to pay heating bills, and there was no heating. I had to pay the water bill, which was also in short supply, electricity, telephone. Then from two banks, the Yugo Banka and Privredna Banka, I had to get certificates and I had to pay for all those certificates. And those certificates said that I was not in debt, that I had no debt. Then also I had to get a certificate from the SUP saying that I was moving. I filled in the forms and my brother's daughter took them in and they gave her a certificate saying that for economic reasons, or something like that, I had to leave Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was that true?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, do you know who is in possession of your home in Prijedor today?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Siljeg moved into the apartment. He was an inspector in the crime department. But I don't know if he's still living there. I have had no contacts with anybody, nor did I ever go to Bosnia or Prijedor either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was that person's ethnicity who moved into the apartment?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how have you survived since leaving Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left Prijedor. I went to another country, a European country, and I got a job. I work. I've been working from the first day I arrived. I did different jobs, as I didn't know the language very well, but now I have learnt the language properly and I can say that I have a good job now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What long-term physical, psychological, emotional effects have you suffered due to your detention in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to describe it, put it into words, but I know that I have no peace anymore, and very often at night I have these terrible images. I hear the screams and the dreadful cries. And to this day I cannot believe that people are capable of doing such things to one another, especially colleagues from work, whom I worked with and lived alongside for such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. We are now going to continue with the testimony and it will be the cross-examination by the Defence counsel. Ms. Susic, do you feel able to continue with the cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Krstan Simic, what will be the order for the cross-examination? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence will be cross-examining in the order of the indictment but in the course of the cross-examination, some of my colleagues might give up their right to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susic, you are now going to be answering questions put to you by the Defence and the questions will be put to you first by Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Simic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Susic.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I apologise to have to take you through those times again but I hope to get through it quickly. In the course of your testimony, you spoke about a work post that was termed leader of the patrol sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a work post titled that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: During your testimony, you also said that it was a work post of a policeman, a police officer who had a little more complicated work assignments than the standard type; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, in the police system set-up, organisation, there were many work posts beginning with the secretary and later on the chief and then down to the ordinary police officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Now, each of these work posts, did they have a description of the job, the assignments that the individual occupying that work post was duty-bound to perform?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had rules and regulations governing salaries, governing --

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Just one moment, Ms. Susic. Let me ask the question first. Did the rules and regulations on salaries, when we would determine personal incomes and points for personal incomes, did it stem from the complexity and type of work performed by each individual employee?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: That means then that every employee had his work duties and would receive remuneration or a salary or personal income from those duties?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, the work post of leader of patrol sector leader, was that work post a post which had the status of a functionary or a senior officer or the chief of a department?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Susic. In your testimony, you also said that you worked in the police force for about 20 years?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the documents that you sent to the Prosecution and the Prosecution handed to the Defence, there is a document that in February of 1992 which said that in February 1992 sometime you were recommended for promotion?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: It is a document where your work was assessed, the assessment of work for employees of the Ministry of the Interior, and it says surname, name, father's name, Susic, Adem, Sifeta. And 21 years of service it says next, particularly excels, and the marks ascribed. You don't remember the document?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll return to the document later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps Ms. Susic could be shown the document she's being asked to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic, it would be a good idea to have the witness shown the document so that she knows what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received this nor do I recognise the signature, Milenko Arapovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, may we have the document placed on the ELMO so we can all get an idea what it is. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, page two relates to your part. The first part is Mr. Arapovic.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never made aware of this. I was never acquainted with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, in the course of the 20 years that you spent working in the police organisation or police system, I'll use that term because the title and heading of the police department changed in various stages, were there any reforms and changes?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were countless ones. I apologise, you mean organisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same department was called by different names in different periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. In the system of the changes that took place, were there any major reorganisational changes in the police structure and system at the end of 1989, and was that system applied on the 1st of January 1990, was it put into practice?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you in concrete specific terms, but I know that it came to be known the police station of Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. You were speaking about the S-U-P, the SUP, and at one point the SUP no longer existed, SUP was dismantled, that's what you said in your testimony, but you kept referring to the organisation of SUP. Now, I would like to know when this reorganisation took place and when the word SUP was no longer used?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I began working in 1971, it was called the Municipal Secretariat for Internal Affairs. Then several years later it became known as the Regional Secretariat for Internal Affairs. Then, it was an intermunicipality SUP. Then the Ministry of the Interior, I think, that was the term it was referred to. So the title of it changed several times but it actually stayed the SUP and the people all knew it as SUP which it was, in fact, and we all knew it as SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When was the term public security station introduced, that title; do you happen to remember?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but I knew that that's what it was referred to, the public security station for traffic, the public security station of Prijedor, that was the term used, and we would usually refer to employees working in the police department as "authorised officials", something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Is it possible that by a legal reorganisation that took place at the end of 1989, the SUP was no longer used and the public security station system established?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, SUPs were never dismantled. It was the same institution but it was called differently, the name changed, I've just explained to you. It was called SUP, but later on it was referred to as the Ministry for Internal Affairs and something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well. But was that something else, the public security station of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station of Prijedor was within the composition of SUP just like all the other police stations that I mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, do you happen to remember who the chief of SUP was in 1989?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1989.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, 1981 [as interpreted] I know that the last one was Hasan Talundzic but perhaps that one was Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Stojanovic whose wife --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Slobodan Stojanovic and his wife Ljilja I know him very well. He was one of the secretaries but when, I can't say exactly, because it wasn't important for me to know the exact dates and the order in which they held those functions but, yes, he was for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What work post did Mr. Scad Besic take up afterwards?
