utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he left and went to Banja Luka or in the security centre. Perhaps he had a function there, I'm not sure, but whether that was before he was chief of SUP in Prijedor or afterwards, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I am going to use the term "public security station" because that was the official term used and this will help us follow the various rules and regulations and so on. Yesterday, you told us about the hierarchy that existed in the public security station. After the democratic parliamentary elections in Bosnia in November 1991, was there any change in the leadership structure within the public security station in keeping with the election results, to reflect the election results?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there were changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Just one moment please who became the chief?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief was Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the public security station, you said yesterday, there were four, shall I say "lines", call them lines.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "lines".

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I mean four organs working in different directions,, the police station in Prijedor, Ljubija. Ms. Susic you have been working in the police force for 21 years, could you please wait for me to put my questions to you because we are talking about organisation and reorganisation of the public security station in which you spent 21 years working.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, yes. The chief was Hasan Talundzic in the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Which other organs, bodies, departments, you can use whichever term you like to make matters easier. What existed in the public security station, what other departments or whatever you like to call them?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- you mean in public security or SUP? I said SUP was made up of the crime department in Prijedor, Ljubija, Omarska, the department, police department in Kozarac, the administrative department, the communications sector. So this wasn't reorganisation which wasn't something that I was preoccupied with. I was telling you on the basis of my recollections. I was never very well acquainted with the organisation, but from what I can remember, it was these departments that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. After the elections who was the chief of the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After the elections who was the commander of the traffic police station?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret Kadiric as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well, Ms. Susic, you always say "as far as you remember" and that's what I am asking you. Who was the chief of the organ in which you worked?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the crime department?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes, but it had a particular name.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the department for the prevention of crime, fire prevention and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well. Who was at the head of that?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mijic Ranko was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you recall who led the fourth department the department for general administration and legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you mentioned an individual called Dule Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And you said that he would go to attend meetings in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that from Fikret Kadiric in an informal conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You also gave an answer yesterday and said that the real chief in the public security station or SUP, which you call SUP was, in fact, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now tell me this: Did Mr. Jankovic, in view of his work post and your own work post, was he your superior?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was Mr. Jankovic a superior to Mr. Fikret Kadiric?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was Mr. Jankovic the superior of Mr. Ranko Mijic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was he superior to Fikret Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was subordinate to Hasan because the number one man in SUP should have been Hasan Talundzic, as all the previous years the secretary or head was always the number one man in SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to dwell for a moment on the police stations which we used to call the militia stations in our former terminology. You said that a police station existed in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You also said that and we're speaking about the basic organisation, that there were other not the traffic one but the basic one, that there were three other police institutions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you tell us their full name, their full status?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was the police station of Ljubija, the police station of Omarska, and the Kozarac police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that in the police station, there was a hierarchy as well, that there was the commander or leader of the station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Furthermore, you stated that he had his deputy?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, he had a deputy, but I'm not sure about the assistants, how many assistants and whether he had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. We're talking about the theoretical formation, theoretical structure, not Omarska. I see that you were focussing on Omarska.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I'm talking about the police station of Ljubija, and the police station of Omarska and they had their commanders or leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I asked you about the police station of Prijedor and that is why I say that I mention that you are not -- you haven't concentrated your attention on that but on something else?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I might have misunderstood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So tell us who the commanders were or superiors were in the -- police station of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the commander, deputy commander and assistant commander as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: We are talking about your knowledge of organisation and not a concrete police force. When we are talking about a department, regardless of which department we're referring to, a department in general, you said that a department had a commander or leader of the police department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The department, police department in Kozarac, that's the -- only the Kozarac one was referred to as a department and had the department leader or commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But, madam, I'm asking you nicely.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't seem to understand you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I think we ought to be able to understand each other. This is my question for you, madam: The police department, a police department, regardless of the place, according to the systematisation and structure that you talked about so much yesterday, did it have the post of commander, deputy and assistant?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the police station of Prijedor, not department, as far as I know and as far as I remember, I know that it was called the police station of Prijedor, the Prijedor police station, and I'm telling you what I know, and I'm 1.000 per cent certain about that -- I'm not 1.000 per cent certain about reorganisation. What I know is that it was called a Prijedor Police Station. It was led by the commander, the deputy commander and the assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's not the department you keep asking me about. That is the police station of Prijedor, not the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now, what I want to ask you is the following: Let us put it in simple terms. A department, any department, whatever, does it have that same hierarchy or organisation structure?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think it's going to be difficult for this witness to respond to an abstract question regarding to any department anywhere, somewhere. Perhaps Mr. Simic could be more specific with his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, would you like to respond to that objection? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the problem is repeating itself. It is very difficult, when we talk about Prosecution witnesses, to establish communication. I asked a question several times, which is a very simple question, and that is: Does the police station department, does it only have a commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I think that it will be difficult for the witness. Your questions are long and repetitive. You repeat what the witness has said. I think that it would be easier if you ask specific, direct questions. And I insist on questions being concise and specific, direct. That is better. You will get a better response. And after all, you know that we all have limited capacity in our reception of information. So break it up into little sections and don't keep repeating either what you have asked or what the witness said or what she said yesterday. So try that way, perhaps. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, the police station department, did it have the same structure as the police station itself had?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer once again: Department, the police department, only existed in Kozarac. That was what it was called. It had its commander. What else it had, I don't know. I don't think that Kozarac department had a deputy, and that was the only one that we referred to as being a department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Susic, how many policemen did departments have?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, we spoke about the changes and reorganisation. Were the departments dismantled, for example? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I should like to have Exhibit 9/1, B/C/S version, and 9/A1, the English version, shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are talking about -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Ms. Susic, may I ask the questions, please, and I think that is where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Everybody wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Simic, go ahead with your questions, but refrain from comments, please. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, this is a decision on the assignment of Mr. Kvocka. To what work post was he assigned to, and where?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this was issued on the 17th of June, 1992, and since the 8th of April, 1992, I had no contact with that service or department. It is quite unknown to me. It's a new decision, new authority, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But does it say here "the Omarska Police Station Department"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "the Public Security Centre Banja Luka, Security Service Centre Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: But the last row.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am reading the title: "The Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Security Service Centre Banja Luka. Date: 17 June 1992. Miroslav Kvocka, worker of the former Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the area of the Serb Republic of BiH, on the day of April 1, 2000, is taken over to work in the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Srpska Republika of B and H and is temporarily assigned until making a regulations book on internal organisation of ..." May I explain, please. It is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, my first question: Is it really necessary to read the document? As you know, it is an exhibit, 9/A1. We are familiar with the document. Is it necessary to repeat and read it here? What is the question that you want to ask the witness? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have asked the witness a very clear question, but the witness wishes to avoid answering that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, to those comments regarding the witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, excuse me. Ask your question. If you want the witness to tell you whether such-and-such is stated in the document, we don't need that. Ask the question you have regarding the document. Another point I wish to make: Make breaks, please, pauses in your conversation; otherwise we are simply not able to follow you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, does this document refer to the police station department?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I wish to comment on this decision myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Madam, I have asked you a very clear question, according to the ruling of this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't give you an answer before I make my comment regarding this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Never mind, then. You don't have to answer my question. Ms. Susic --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: We were talking about work posts. Who was assigning persons to work posts within the police structure, according to this decision?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the secretary of the SUP assigned people to work posts. I know it from my own experience. In my decision, it was Mr. Panic who assigned me to a work post, and I worked there for 21 years, and I think that the decisions I received were always signed by the secretary. He was the person who assigned workers to various work posts. I had the good or bad luck, I don't know, to have the one and the same work post throughout. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Could we please show D8/1 and D8/1A, the English version. Could this exhibit be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Have you had time to look through this decision?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who issued this decision?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who signed the decision?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs, Mirko Topalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is regulated by this decision?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that Miroslav Kvocka is appointed to the post of leader of the patrol sector, leader of the patrol sector of the region. That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you still maintain that the assignment to work posts was done by the secretary?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am quite sure that the secretary of every SUP made its proposal and opinion, and it was a mere formality that the republican secretary would sign the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My question is: Who issues the decision?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't understand you. I didn't necessarily have to know that. Personally, I don't think that is important anyway, regardless of who signs a decision, whether it would be my boss or the SUP secretary or the republican secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could Mr. Kvocka become deputy police commander if there was no such decision signed by the minister, regardless of who gave the proposal?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I said that as far as I recollected, in those stations there was a commander and a deputy commander, and that as far as I can remember, the commander in Omarska was Zeljko Meakic and his deputy Miroslav Kvocka. I always said "as far as I can recollect." That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, let us dwell for a moment on Omarska. Do you know a person called Radovan Daljevic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to work in the police station somewhere, but I don't know exactly what his job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know, or rather you mentioned a person called Milutin Bujic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know what his job was in the police?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. I know he was a uniformed officer. I think he was working in the Prijedor police station. That is what I think, as far as I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Osme Didovic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the police station department in Kozarac, which unfortunately no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you know a person called Branko Bjekic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Bjekic, yes. He was the commander of the police station department in Ljubija. He was a Croat. As far as I know, he did sign loyalty to the Serb authorities, but unfortunately he ended up in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know any single commander from Omarska prior to the mentioned Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the police station department in Omarska was Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know any others in the past 20 years?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It wasn't important for me to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And finally, let me go back to the questions that I have already referred to. Members of the police organisation, were they under military obligation?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, when giving a statement, I said that in the past 20 or so years that I worked, we did have military exercises, and we all had decisions on assignments in the case of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who issued those assignments?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to explain this to you, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My question is your particular position. You were working as an assistant or an employee, a clerk. What was your duty in case of war?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be -- it said. My decision said that I would be appointed to keeping the criminal records.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does that mean the same post as you had in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said that this applied to all persons in the police.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to the majority of workers. Those exercises --

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm not talking about exercises; I'm talking about decisions. So the head of the -- the chief of the police, I assume, would have to, in time of war, would have to perform the duties of police chief. So the Prosecutor described this as a parallel work post. Did you have two jobs or one?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And the commander of the police station, if he had a wartime obligation to continue to be commander of the police station, was he performing two work posts or one?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but if a war breaks out, it is his duty to report to the post he has been assigned to, and that means that he would carry out the same duties as he had in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. All members of the police force knew what their obligations were in case of war?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, you said that you spent most of your time in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did you go downstairs?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, after we got up, between 6.00 and 7.00. Whether it was half past 6.00 or 6.00, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did you go back to the sleeping room?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, about half past 6.00 or 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You referred to two rooms upstairs. Was anything written on one of the doors of those two rooms; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: With the exception of the interrogations, during the stay of the interrogators, from 7.00 to 7.00, during those 12 hours, did you go upstairs to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One morning I came to clean the hall, the last room on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: A room for meetings?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They called it a hall. I cleaned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Nada Markovska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was she?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a typist in the crime department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Nevenka Sikman?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. She was also a typist in the crime department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did they come to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know in which room they worked during the day?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there during the day, except once. One morning before they started working, the inspectors came to the hall and breakfast was served and I was cleaning the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So you don't know who worked in which of these rooms during the daytime, during the working hours. Thank you. I have no further questions. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I have a couple of other questions for you first. Could I ask the usher for his assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, I'm going to show you now a document and to ask you to look at it, please. Ms. Susic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, wait a moment so that we can have the document and have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the B/C/S it's D28/1. For the English version it's D28/1A. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you to wait until we got copies. We have the copies of the document now. You may continue, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, did you give statements to the investigators of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have before you the witness statement?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are the dates indicated when you made the statement?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember the dates. I didn't take note of the dates, but that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does it say the 5th and the 12th of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, if that is what it says, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And the 26th of February, 1995. Did you give that statement of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How many hours a day did you work on that statement?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You have the English version in front of you. Does your signature figure on the first page?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does your signature appear on every page?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my initial. I don't even remember signing every page but --

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, I see some corrections even in the text.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was that statement read to you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was read to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: At the end of the statement, did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but I remember on two occasions that I had certain observations regarding errors in the translation because some things had been mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Is your signature on the last page?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the last page?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which last page you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The last page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes, but you'll find it on the last as well of the English version.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on the last page. Yes, yes, up there, sorry, I'm sorry, yes. It's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, were you telling the truth then?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have always told the truth and I will always tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In view of the time when you gave that statement, did you recollect the events better then, the events of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember now I remembered well then, and I still remember quite well what I said in my statement, but I wish to note that I did notice an error in the translation of these statements and that I commented on them. There were several translators and they may have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I apologise, you have the witness here in front of you. Ask what you want now. You have the document. You have you have the statement. Put your question, the question you want to put to the witness. It's a good thing to have the witness here in front of you so ask her what you want. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have ended with the cross-examination, and I would like in line with the instructions of Judge Wald that attention be paid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. Simic. I don't have the translation but that now is not the moment to make allegations regarding the testimony. You can do that at the end of the trial. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I had not intended to do that. I just intended to draw attention to certain parts of the statement that will be used rather than the whole statement because it is very lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we must discuss that matter tomorrow at the Status Conference so we're going to come back to that, but there's always certain incoherence there because there's a problem. There are some people who object to the admission of these statements into evidence and others who are in favour so we must be consistent or we must establish the conditions under which these statements will be used. But in any event, we have already said that the principle is the presence of the witness and the principle of orality but I don't want to take any more time now. Have you finished with your cross-examination? Are you going to ask her for the admission of this exhibit? Very well, we'll see at the end, fine. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Simic. I think it is now time for a break. So we're going to have a half-hour break. I see that the witness has something to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I really wish to make my comment regarding the decision given to me by Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I think that Mr. Simic had no other questions about it so you can't give us answers unless there is a question addressed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is very important for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see. We'll see. Will the usher please escort the witness out so that she can leave before us. So we're going to have a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Mr. Nikolic, I take it that you have no questions because I see Mr. Fila in the row in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, our Defence team has decided not to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Ms. Susic, you will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila, your witness. Don't forget to make pauses, Mr. Fila, between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Sivac [sic] I'm going to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is Susic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do apologise, yes, Ms. Susic, I will be brief. Are you sure that at some relevant point in time, and we're talking about the time that is important for us here, 1992 or a little before that, that the police station in Omarska was not the department of the police station of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know that it was the Omarska police station all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So in 1992, you don't -- you say that it was not a police station department?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was working in SUP, that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So in the transformation from SUP to the public security station, you maintain that Omarska remained a police station?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My next question: Are you absolutely certain that at the relevant time for the indictment, once again, 1992, and the time that you worked there, that it had a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was to the best of my recollection. I'm certain about the commander. I know he existed. As far as I can remember, there was a deputy, but I said that I wasn't sure about the assistants. So there had to be a deputy commander but I can't claim that 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us assume, then, that it was the police station department, did it have to have a deputy. It wasn't a department, had it been a department --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kozarac department only had the commander of the department, department commander of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I say that the difference between the police station and the police station department is that the department is smaller than the police station proper?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And therefore, the commander of the police station department perhaps did not have a deputy because it was not necessary?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From the time you left your active duty and employment up until the 24th of June, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You lived at home?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that two offices in the administration building were used on the first floor by the guards.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You enumerated some of those individuals, and amongst them was- Mlado Radic. Was one of them perhaps -- did it have a radio transmitter and telephone?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember but I think I saw something like that there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have to interrupt. I believe the witness' testimony was that two offices in the administration building were used by the commanders of the guards, not by the ordinary guards themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the persons that she said had used the offices. I accept if that is what you understood as well, and she mentioned the individuals who used the premises, and I just asked whether in one of those two offices, there was a radio station, transmitter or telephone. I didn't say that all the guards used those offices just to clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned Mlado Radic and you said that you assumed what he did there. Now, what post -- what was the place where the conversation between you and Mlado Radic took place? It's an open session so that you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the corridor between the kitchen and the toilet, behind the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean on the ground floor or on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ground floor behind the kitchen. The kitchen was on the ground floor in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning and breakfast was being served.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How far were the other people who were there?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several other women in the kitchen perhaps two, but there was a wall partition and no one was there when I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After that conversation, did Mlado Radic undertake anything in the sense of ...

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know Ranko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he bring you anything?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He brought me several changes of underclothing, three, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with him? Did he ask you something, did you answer something, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. He took me out, he would usually come in the evening. This was not once, it was several times. He would peek through the door in the evening, I don't know the exact time. I was the last one under the window and he would make a sign with to me with his finger like this and say, "Sifeta come over here." And I remember one of the conversations, it was one in one of the offices up on the first floor, I don't remember which one. He took me there and he said that he too was surprised why I had not signed a loyalty to the Serb authorities, and I repeated what I said to Zeljko, and that's where that conversation ended and I remember that particular discussion. The next time I remember him coming when he brought me my underclothes. He told me that he was coming back from Banja Luka and usually he would be under the effects of alcohol. I remember that I told him about my problems as far as hygiene was concerned and the sanitary material that I needed, and I said that I had only one change of underclothes and he brought me three fresh changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Not to lose too much time. Did he ask you how you were, whether anybody was abusing you, beating you or anything? Did he ask you anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Bozidar Markovic, a guard?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not acquainted with that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In front of your rooms, the rooms you slept in, was there a guard on a bench, sitting on a bench of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bench was on the left-hand side of the landing, because the first office was a little smaller, which meant that there was a landing and that there was a bench there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was somebody sitting on that bench, one of those guards, to watch over you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't one. There were usually several, two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could anybody go into your room without the guards seeing him?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the guards were there, of course this could not happen. They would have to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. That completes my questioning of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness. We shall not be cross-examining her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Tosic. Thank you very much. Mr. Jovan Simic has the floor. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, was Mr. Prcac an active-duty policeman at the beginning of the war conflicts in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not an active-duty policeman at all. He was a crime technician. And I don't know how long before the war he retired as a crime technician and not an active-duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: Do you know when he retired?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: Was that immediately before the war broke out or a long time before that?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A long time prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: Was it true that Zeljko Meakic was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat his question, please. We did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him every day, but I saw him frequently. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: Did you see Zeljko Meakic during the night? Did he sleep in Omarska at night?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where he slept. I would see him from 7.00, when we went up to the rooms, and if I happened to go to the toilet, I might meet him in the hallway, because the doors to one of these offices was open and I was able to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether Drago Prcac helped any of the women by bringing food, clothing, or medicines?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That was my first meeting with Drago Prcac. I happened to be in the restaurant. I was sitting down and I suddenly saw Prcac coming from the "glass house" towards the women, and he was carrying a plastic bag with him. At that particular moment I felt happy because I thought that Drago was bringing me the plastic bag, perhaps some food inside or something else. But he came up to me, he didn't look me in the eyes, and I looked him in the eyes directly and he asked me, "Siva, who is Cikota?" And I indicated with my hands Zlata Cikota. But in the meantime she said, "It's me. I'm Cikota." And he gave her the plastic bag and then I saw Zlata take something out of the plastic bag and eat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: Did you meet Drago after you left Omarska in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: In the restaurant, on the ground floor, apart from the entrance that you indicated, from the backside, that is to say from the wall partition, looking towards the "white house," is there any other exit, any other way out?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the hallway that I mentioned, where the table was and where some people were having breakfast, there was a door leading outside that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: Was there any other exit, any other way out that led to another section?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the main entrance and this other entrance, and there was a door towards the "glass house," if you mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. J
utterances.text: But no, I mean out of the building.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just those two doors leading outside. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovan Simic. Mr. Saxon, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, when you were working for the crime department within the SUP in Prijedor, what were the other two parts of the organisation known as the SUP? There was the crime department that you worked for, and what were the other two main parts?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the police station, the department for administrative matters, the police station for traffic, and the communications centre. All those sections made up the Secretariat for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, there was a separate department known as the crime department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And a separate department known as the police department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was the traffic section contained within the police department?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was separate, because those commanders, those leaders, were neither superior nor subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And then there was an administration and communication department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So all together, then, the SUP contained four primary departments; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You've explained that in the first part of 1992 the secretary of the SUP was a man named Hasan Talundzic, and as you put it, Hasan Talundzic was the number one man at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But during that first part of 1992, who effectively became the number one man in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I learnt in talking to Fikret Kadiric, that the commander, the then-commander of the police station, Dusan Jankovic, frequently went to Banja Luka, to the centre of the Security Services, using the official vehicle, and not informing Hasan Talundzic of his trip, and Hasan Talundzic was the chief of SUP. And this was something that was unthinkable previously. If the official car was to be used, the superior had to be asked to use it; not locally around Prijedor, but for any longer distance you had to sign for fuel, et cetera, so you had to receive authorisation to use the official vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Susic, you described how prior to the armed conflict that began in 1992, you and your colleagues occasionally had to perform military -- had to participate, rather, in military exercises, and that in case of war you would have performed the same position that you performed in peacetime. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When the armed conflict began in the Prijedor area around May of 1992, you weren't able to continue in your former job, were you?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on sick leave from the 9th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Muslim employees were dismissed from their jobs at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a telephone conversation with Aga Sadikovic, several days after the Serb authorities took control, the Serbs took control, I talked to Aga. I don't remember whether he phoned me or I phoned him, but I do know for sure that we talked on that first day when he went to work. He told me that he had come to the stairs of the SUP building, that a flag was hung out with the three S's sign. It was put up on the building. I don't remember who of the personnel were on the stairs, but they disarmed him. They took his pistol. He was a civilian himself, in fact, but he had a pistol. And this person said that workers of non-Serb ethnicity could not enter the building, and of course he never went to the building after that. And had I gone, the same thing would have happened to me. But as I say, I was on sick leave at the time, and so I didn't need to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to the events when you were detained in the Omarska camp, you mentioned that one morning you were told to clean up a large room on the left-hand side on the first floor. What, if anything, did you find in that room?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find anything in that room. I cleaned it. On the table was the breakfasts, on large trays. And my colleagues, my colleagues from work, would come into the room. They didn't say anything to me. I felt very uncomfortable to clean up around them without a single word being uttered. And when I finished cleaning, I left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that the breakfasts were on the large trays, were these the breakfasts that were eaten by the interrogators at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was the breakfast eaten by the interrogators at Omarska different or the same as the breakfasts or meals eaten by the prisoners the Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they couldn't be compared. I remember that they had salami and cheese laid out and small brioches and bread; whereas the food we ate, I said it was everything but food. It didn't resemble food at all; it was more something that you would give to cattle. And sometimes it was moldy and had gone bad, and there was only one or two plastic spoons per plate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, when you say that "they" had salami and cheese laid out, who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the interrogators, my colleagues from work, and they were mostly there that morning. I remember Vukasin Knezevic. He was there. Then there was Nebojsa Tomcic, Nebojsa Babic, Mijic, Ranko. There were some others. I think there was a Zoric, who was a professor, a teacher. But I remember these people very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would the camp commanders that you saw, and the camp guards, eat the same food that the interrogators ate?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the guards. I never saw them eating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What about the --

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except that one time, the time I discussed, the occasion I described, on a Saturday or a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. A few moments ago you were shown a copy of a statement that you signed in February of 1995, and you said that before you signed that statement, it was read back to you. Was it read back to you in a language that you understood?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that it was actually read back to me. When I answered questions, the translator translated into English. When everything had been completed, perhaps it was read out. I don't remember exactly. I just know I signed it. But I do remember the following conversation. I don't know the date this took place, but it was when the investigator who talked to me repeated some things, and I reacted and said, "That is not what I said. I didn't say that." And then he said, or she said -- I don't remember whether it was a woman or man -- they said that this was probably a mistake in the translation, because sometimes it was difficult to translate from English into my own language, and that it was quite possible that there were mistakes. But I can explain everything that I said and stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. In the offices that were across the hall from the rooms where the women slept at Omarska, were those offices used by camp commanders and people in authority or were those offices used by ordinary guards?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said several times that in those offices, I saw Zeljko Meakic, Mlado Radic, Miroslav Kvocka, Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned an incident when you saw Drago Prcac approach you with a plastic bag and he asked you, "Siva, who is Cikota?"

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes, but he wasn't looking me in the eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is the first name of the person that he referred -- that Mr. Prcac referred to as "Cikota"?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlata.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know if Zlata Cikota was married at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know the name of her husband?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sead Cikota, the person who was in the camp at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Susic, when you went to Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic to see if they could help you get some antibiotics or some hygienic supplies, and in the beginning they said they were sorry, they couldn't help you, did either one refer to you anyone else in the camp and say, "Well, go see this other person, because they are the ones who are in charge of the hygiene or they are the ones who are in charge of the medical treatment"? Did they suggest that you bring your request to anybody else in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My second question is: After the incident with Mr. Radic, did you tell anybody at that time at the camp about that? Or if not, when was the first time you told anybody about that incident?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was maybe a year ago. Nusret Sivac, my colleague, who was retired when the war began, came for a visit. He was travelling through the town I was living in and he came to see me and we talked about those terrible days. I know I started crying and I told him this. He told this to an investigator when he talked to him, and the next time I was questioned about that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did any of the women that were in the same sleeping rooms as you were, and you said sometimes women might be called out at night, did any of them ever discuss among themselves their experiences with any sexual advances that might have been made upon them, or did they not discuss it?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't talk about it, except for one woman, who told me one evening, whispering, that a guard -- and she showed him to me. I think his name was Lugar. He had a red face and he wore a moustache -- "He would sometimes come to our room and show us a photograph of his daughter." She told me that he had taken her to a room under the steps and ordered her to lift her dress or whatever it was she was wearing, and when he saw that she was bleeding, he told her, "As soon as it stops, let me know." She was telling me this through tears and asking me whether she should report it to Zeljko Meakic. I said, "You decide, but try." And afterwards she told me that she had gone to Meakic and told him about it and he said, "I will move him away from here." However, that didn't happen. The guard was still there in the corridor in the restaurant, I would see him, and I don't know exactly after how long the same event was repeated. She told me again and as she was still bleeding, that was all that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question is you said after the incident you didn't talk to Mr. Radic ever again. Did you come into contact with him ever or often during your remaining time at the camp, did he ever approach you again or did you have no contact with each other the rest of the time?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember ever talking to him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susic, you have answered a question regarding differences in the breakfasts that were served. Were there other differences regarding other meals?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. You are referring to what the detainees were eating?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the breakfast of the investigators was quite different from the breakfast that prisoners had so my question is what about the other meals? Was there a difference between the food ate by prisoners and the food ate by guards?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they didn't eat with us detainees. It was only on that one occasion that I saw what the inspectors were having for breakfast when I was in this big room and I saw, as I described, when I was in the corridor, that the breakfast was normal. As for the prisoners, they ate something that didn't look like food. Sometimes the piece of bread they would get would be moldy and green. I remember I couldn't eat at all the first few days because I couldn't, and I was hungry, and I remember a guard pushing me with a rifle or something and said, "Eat," and I had to eat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did the meal of the prisoners consist of?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A piece of bread, a quarter of a loaf, sometimes less, and a kind of cooked vegetable. It was very watery, sometimes there would be some peas, sometimes some meat, which was very rarely the case. I never poured the food. I washed the dishes, the plates, but had I occasion to see the food, two spoonfuls of something. It was a plastic plate, a flat one, and there was very little food in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned that you worked in the restaurant and in the kitchen. Did you spend more time in one of these than in the other or was it equally divided between the kitchen and the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SIFETA SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't work in the restaurant, we were sitting there, and the women who went to the kitchen to work, one of them would pour the food to the detainees into plates, and I was always washing the plates and collecting the empty plates returned by the detainees. I remember once that I had to clean all the tiles in the kitchen. I would wash the floors too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Susic. You have answered all our questions. I don't know whether you have anything to say that you haven't had the opportunity to say so far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appeal to you to give me the possibility to express my opinion about this decision shown to me by the gentleman whose name I have forgotten who gave it to me to see and read. I am appealing to you once again though you denied me that request earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Ms. Susic, I'm afraid I cannot because no one has asked you a question about it. If you wish to make a statement, but regarding other questions, the matter is closed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much for coming, Ms. Susic. You are a very brave woman and we wish you a safe journey to your home, to your place of residence, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have another matter to deal with regarding the exhibits. Mr. Saxon. I'm sorry, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time, the Prosecution would ask that the following exhibits be admitted into evidence: Exhibit 3/99, Exhibit 3/100, Exhibit 3/101, and although, Your Honour -- I realise this matter of statements and admission of statements will be addressed tomorrow at the Status Conference, we would like to reserve our rights to have admitted the statement signed by Sifeta Susic in February 1995 which was shown to her by Mr. Simic today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I don't know whether you are speaking on behalf of all the counsel regarding the exhibits which the Prosecutor wishes to tender, and what is your position regarding the Exhibit 28/1? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I speak on behalf of all the Defence. We have no objections regarding the proposal of the Prosecution regarding their exhibits; however, in expectation of tomorrow's status meeting, we also wanted conditionally to tender the statements of Ms. Susic, of the 5th, 12th and 26th into evidence, but we wished only to highlight certain parts of that statement; that is, page five, under the heading "Omarska", the first and second paragraph; on page seven, the heading is "Camp Commanders", and on page eight, the third paragraph. And we would like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to those paragraphs for their consideration in making their judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Exhibits tendered by the Prosecutor are admitted, and we will delay the amission of Exhibit 28 because we will be discussing that matter tomorrow. Now, Mr. Niemann, I think you were going to say that this is not the best moment to begin with another witness. Isn't that so, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, it's getting very close, Your Honour, to the adjournment. I'm in Your Honour's hands. We can start if you would like to, but it's entirely a matter for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's really no point in starting the testimony for five minutes, so we will be here tomorrow at 9.30 and we will begin then. So for today, the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
